newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria unveils five political parties.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria unveils five political parties.

text.p: Five political parties were registered in Nigeria on Monday for the transition to civilian rule, three years after another attempt ended in failure when the military scrapped presidential polls.
The five, out of 15 aspiring parties, all occupy the political centre ground and leave the opposition aside.

"All political associations that have not qualified for registration are hereby dissolved," said electoral commission chairman Sumner Dagogo-Jack, as he announced the registrations in the capital Abuja.
The announcement is one step toward military ruler General Sani Abacha's promise of a handover to an elected president in 1998.
On Monday Abacha laid the foundation stone for a new 5.46 billion naira ($68 million) parliament building that will house an elected national assembly.
"This is the practical demonstration to show that our transition programme is on course," he said.
Nigerian opposition groups and Western governments, demanding Abacha hand over power sooner than he intends, remain unimpressed with the transition programme.

Abacha's government, seen as a pariah by much of the international community after it executed nine minority rights activists in November, insists it will follow its own course to democracy and will not be railroaded by any external pressures.

The Commonwealth, a grouping of Britain and its former colonies and protectorates, suspended Nigeria last November after the executions but on Sunday decided not to apply sanctions to maintain dialogue with the oil-rich state.
Aspiring parties had to scale hurdles that included having at least 40,000 members in each of Nigeria's 30 states.
Among those that failed to qualify is the People's Progressive Party made up mainly of members of the opposition National Democratic Coalition (NADECO).
NADECO propelled millionaire businessman Moshood Abiola to declare himself president in 1994 based on the results in an annulled 1993 poll that he is widely believed to have won.
The annulment plunged Nigeria into its worst political crisis since the 30-month civil war that ended in 1970 and in which one million people were killed.
Abiola remains in detention and the opposition has been decimated by the detention or flight of pro-democracy and human rights activists.

The programme itself is behind schedule on delineating constituencies and compiling a voters' register but the chairman of the electoral commission has maintained that this would not affect the handover date.
A similar elaborate plan by the previous military government collapsed when the 1993 election was annulled.
The five parties registered are the United Nigeria Congress Party, Committee for National Consensus, National Centre Party of Nigeria, Democratic Party of Nigeria and Grassroot Democratic Movement.
